prompt: What is a hydrogen bond?

choices.text: An attraction between a hydrogen bonded to a strongly electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom
The covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms in H2
choices.why: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force, a special dipole–dipole attraction, not a covalent bond.

choices.text: Any bond that contains a hydrogen atom
choices.why: C–H bonds, for example, don't make hydrogen bonds. The hydrogen must be bonded to a strongly electronegative atom and near a lone pair on another.

choices.text: An ionic bond between H^+ and an anion
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds are weaker than true ionic bonds. They're a special type of dipole–dipole attraction.

explanation: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole–dipole attraction that forms when a hydrogen atom bonded to a strongly electronegative atom is near another electronegative atom with a lone pair of electrons.

prompt: How strong is a hydrogen bond compared with other forces?

choices.text: Stronger than ordinary dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, but about a tenth of an average covalent bond
Stronger than covalent bonds
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds are weaker than true covalent and ionic bonds, about a tenth of the strength of an average covalent bond.

choices.text: Weaker than dispersion forces
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds are generally stronger than ordinary dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

choices.text: About the same as an ionic bond
choices.why: Hydrogen bonds are weaker than true ionic and covalent bonds.

explanation: Hydrogen bonds are generally stronger than ordinary dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, but weaker than true covalent and ionic bonds: about a tenth of the strength of an average covalent bond. In liquid water they are constantly broken and reformed.

prompt: Boiling points of the group 14 hydrides rise steadily down the group. For groups 15, 16, and 17, which hydrides break the pattern with abnormally high boiling points?

choices.text: NH3, H2O, and HF
PH3, H2S, and HCl
choices.why: These follow the normal trend. It's the first member of each group, NH3, H2O, and HF, whose boiling point is abnormally high.

choices.text: CH4, SiH4, and GeH4
choices.why: These are group 14 hydrides, which rise steadily with no anomaly.

choices.text: The heaviest hydride in each group
choices.why: The heaviest follow the normal trend. The first member of each group, NH3, H2O, and HF, is the exception.

explanation: In groups 15–17, the hydride of the first element in each group (NH3, H2O, and HF) has an abnormally high boiling point, which requires additional intermolecular forces: hydrogen bonds.

prompt: Why do the boiling points of the group 14 hydrides (CH4, SiH4, and so on) increase down the group?

choices.text: The molecules get larger with more electrons, so dispersion forces get stronger
Hydrogen bonding gets stronger down the group
choices.why: Group 14 hydrides don't hydrogen bond. Their boiling points rise because dispersion forces grow with molecular size.

choices.text: The molecules become more polar
choices.why: The rise comes from larger molecules with more electrons, which have stronger van der Waals dispersion forces.

explanation: Going down group 14, the hydride molecules get larger with more electrons, so van der Waals dispersion forces become greater and boiling points rise.

prompt: Why are the lone pairs on N, O, and F especially good at hydrogen bonding?

choices.text: At the 2-level, they are in a small volume of space, so their negative charge density is high
N, O, and F have more lone pairs than any other atoms
choices.why: It's not the number but the charge density: 2-level lone pairs are compact and strongly negative.

choices.text: Their lone pairs are more diffuse than those of larger atoms
choices.why: The reverse: lone pairs at higher levels are more diffuse, with lower charge density.

choices.text: N, O, and F are positively charged
choices.why: These highly electronegative atoms carry a partial negative charge, concentrated in compact 2-level lone pairs.

explanation: Lone pairs at the 2-level hold their electrons in a relatively small volume of space, giving a high negative charge density. Lone pairs at higher levels are more diffuse, with lower charge density and less affinity for positive charge.

prompt: How many hydrogen bonds can one water molecule potentially form with surrounding water molecules?
explanation: A water molecule has two δ+ hydrogens to donate and two lone pairs on oxygen to accept, so it can form four hydrogen bonds: two through its hydrogens and two through its oxygen's lone pairs.

prompt: Why does water have a higher boiling point than both ammonia and hydrogen fluoride?

choices.text: Water has exactly enough hydrogens and lone pairs for every one of them to hydrogen bond
Water has the largest molar mass of the three
choices.why: HF (20 g/mol) is heavier than water (18 g/mol), yet water boils higher, because it forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule.

choices.text: Water is the only one of the three that hydrogen bonds
choices.why: All three hydrogen bond. Ammonia is short of lone pairs and HF short of hydrogens; water has the right numbers of both.

choices.text: Oxygen is the most electronegative of the three
choices.why: Fluorine is more electronegative. Water wins because its two hydrogens and two lone pairs can all take part.

explanation: Each nitrogen in ammonia has only one lone pair, so there aren't enough lone pairs for all the hydrogens. HF is short of hydrogens. Water, with two hydrogens and two lone pairs, has exactly the right numbers, making it an ideal hydrogen-bonded system.

prompt: When an ionic substance dissolves, how does water attach to the negative ions?

choices.text: Through hydrogen bonds to the anion's lone pairs
Through coordinate (dative covalent) bonds from oxygen
choices.why: Water frequently attaches to positive ions that way. It bonds to negative ions through hydrogen bonds.

choices.text: It doesn't attach to negative ions
choices.why: Water clusters around both kinds of ion: negative ions through hydrogen bonds.

explanation: Water frequently attaches to positive ions by coordinate (dative covalent) bonds, and to negative ions by hydrogen bonds. Chloride's lone pairs are at the 3-level and normally too diffuse, but the full negative charge makes them attractive enough.

prompt: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and methoxymethane (CH3OCH3) have the same formula, C2H6O. Why does ethanol boil about 100 °C higher?

choices.text: Ethanol has a hydrogen bonded directly to oxygen, so it can hydrogen bond; methoxymethane can't
Ethanol has more electrons
choices.why: Both have the formula C2H6O, so they have the same number of electrons and similar van der Waals forces.

choices.text: Methoxymethane's oxygen has no lone pairs
choices.why: Methoxymethane's oxygen still has its lone pairs. What it lacks is a hydrogen attached to oxygen with enough δ+ charge.

choices.text: Ethanol is a much longer molecule
choices.why: The two have a similar length. The difference is ethanol's O–H group, which allows hydrogen bonding.

explanation: The two molecules have the same number of electrons and similar van der Waals attractions. Ethanol has a hydrogen attached directly to oxygen and can hydrogen bond; in methoxymethane the hydrogens aren't δ+ enough. Ethanol boils at 78.5 °C, methoxymethane at −24.8 °C.

prompt: Ethanol boils at 78.5 °C and methoxymethane at −24.8 °C. By how many degrees does hydrogen bonding raise ethanol's boiling point above methoxymethane's?
explanation: 78.5 °C − (−24.8 °C) = 103.3 °C, the "about 100 °C" lift the section attributes to hydrogen bonding.

prompt: Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol both have an –OH group. Why is the boiling point of 2-methylpropan-1-ol lower?

choices.text: Its branching makes van der Waals attractions less effective
It can't hydrogen bond
choices.why: Both alcohols have an –OH group and hydrogen bond. The difference comes from branching weakening van der Waals attractions.

choices.text: It has fewer electrons
choices.why: The two are isomers with the same number of electrons. Branching makes their van der Waals attractions less effective.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding exists in addition to van der Waals attractions. Both alcohols hydrogen bond, but the branching in 2-methylpropan-1-ol makes its van der Waals attractions less effective than in the longer butan-1-ol.

prompt: In a hydrogen bond, what are the donor and the acceptor?

choices.text: The donor is an electronegative atom (N, O, or F) bonded to the H; the acceptor is an electronegative atom with a lone pair
The donor is the atom with the lone pair; the acceptor is the H
choices.why: The donor is the electronegative atom covalently bonded to the hydrogen. The acceptor contributes the lone pair.

choices.text: Both are hydrogen atoms
choices.why: A hydrogen bond links a hydrogen on the donor (N, O, or F) to a lone pair on an electronegative acceptor atom.

choices.text: The donor is always a metal ion
choices.why: The donor is usually a strongly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F, covalently bonded to the hydrogen.

explanation: The donor is usually a strongly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) covalently bonded to a hydrogen atom, which it leaves partly positive. The acceptor is an electronegative atom of a neighboring molecule or ion with a lone pair that takes part in the hydrogen bond.

prompt: What is an intramolecular hydrogen bond?

choices.text: A hydrogen bond between a donor and an acceptor within one molecule, as between the two –OH groups of ethylene glycol
A hydrogen bond between two separate molecules
choices.why: That's an intermolecular hydrogen bond. "Intra" means within one molecule.

choices.text: The covalent O–H bond itself
choices.why: The covalent bond to hydrogen is the donor's bond. An intramolecular hydrogen bond links that H to an acceptor elsewhere in the same molecule.

explanation: Intramolecular hydrogen bonds occur within one molecule, when a hydrogen donor and acceptor are close to each other in it, as with the two hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol. Intermolecular hydrogen bonds occur between separate molecules.

prompt: H2O (18 g/mol) boils at 373 K and HF (20 g/mol) at 292.5 K. Why does the lighter molecule boil higher?

choices.text: Water takes part in more hydrogen bonds per molecule
Heavier molecules always boil lower
choices.why: Usually larger molar mass means higher boiling point. Water is an exception because it forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule.

choices.text: HF doesn't hydrogen bond
choices.why: HF does hydrogen bond. Water simply forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule.

choices.text: Water has stronger dispersion forces
choices.why: Dispersion forces grow with molar mass, which favors HF. Water's extra hydrogen bonds win.

explanation: We usually expect larger molar mass to mean a higher boiling point, because of greater dispersion forces. But H2O, although lighter than HF, takes part in more hydrogen bonds per molecule, so its boiling point is higher.

prompt: How does hydrogen bonding affect viscosity?

choices.text: Substances that hydrogen bond tend to be more viscous, especially those that form multiple hydrogen bonds
Hydrogen bonding lowers viscosity
choices.why: The effect matches the effect on boiling point: hydrogen bonding makes substances more viscous.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding has no effect on viscosity
choices.why: Substances that form hydrogen bonds tend to have higher viscosity.

explanation: Substances capable of forming hydrogen bonds tend to have higher viscosity than those that don't, and substances that can form multiple hydrogen bonds have even higher viscosities.

prompt: PH3 has the same trigonal pyramidal shape as NH3, but it doesn't hydrogen bond. Why?

choices.text: Phosphorus and hydrogen have similar electronegativities, so H gets no significant partial positive charge
PH3 has no lone pair
choices.why: PH3 has a lone pair, like NH3. The problem is that its hydrogens aren't δ+ enough.

choices.text: PH3 is too light
choices.why: PH3 (34 g/mol) is heavier than NH3. It can't hydrogen bond because P and H have similar electronegativities.

choices.text: Phosphorus is more electronegative than nitrogen
choices.why: Nitrogen is more electronegative. Phosphorus's electronegativity is close to hydrogen's, so the P–H bond leaves H without a useful δ+ charge.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs a significant electronegativity difference between hydrogen and the atom it's bonded to. Phosphorus and hydrogen both have electronegativities of about 2.1, so the hydrogen doesn't acquire the partial positive charge needed to hydrogen bond.

prompt: Why does chlorine form hydrogen bonds poorly, despite being quite electronegative?

choices.text: It is large, so the nuclei can't get close enough for a strong interaction
It has no lone pairs
choices.why: Chlorine has lone pairs. Its large size keeps donor and acceptor nuclei too far apart.

choices.text: It is less electronegative than hydrogen
choices.why: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen. Its size is what limits its hydrogen bonding.

explanation: The size of donors and acceptors affects hydrogen bonding. When the radii of the two atoms differ greatly or are large, their nuclei can't come close when they interact, so the interaction is weak. This accounts for chlorine's relatively low ability to form hydrogen bonds.

prompt: What holds the two strands of the DNA double helix together?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonds between N–H hydrogens on one strand and N or O lone pairs on the other
Covalent bonds between the strands
choices.why: The strands are held by hydrogen bonds, which are weaker than covalent bonds and can be broken and reformed.

choices.text: Ionic bonds between metal ions
choices.why: The strands are held by hydrogen bonds between N–H groups and lone pairs on N or O.

choices.text: Dispersion forces alone
choices.why: The section credits hydrogen bonds between hydrogens on nitrogen and lone pairs on nitrogen or oxygen.

explanation: The two strands of DNA's double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen on one strand and lone pairs on another nitrogen or an oxygen on the other.

prompt: How does hydrogen bonding help plants move water up from their roots?

choices.text: Water hydrogen bonds to itself and to cellulose in the vessel walls, enabling capillary action and long chains of water
Water forms covalent bonds to cellulose
choices.why: The attraction is hydrogen bonding, to each other and to the cellulose walls, which lets water rise by capillary action.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonds break, letting water flow freely upward
choices.why: It's the attraction from hydrogen bonds, among water molecules and to cellulose, that pulls water up.

explanation: In the cohesion–adhesion theory, water in a plant's xylem hydrogen bonds to other water molecules and to the cellulose walls, creating capillary action. Hydrogen bonding can form long chains of water molecules that overcome gravity and reach the leaves.

prompt: In the secondary structure of proteins, hydrogen bonds form mainly between which groups?

choices.text: N–H hydrogens on one polypeptide backbone and oxygen atoms on a neighboring one
C–H hydrogens and carbon atoms
choices.why: Carbon isn't electronegative enough. The bonds are between N–H hydrogens and backbone oxygens.

choices.text: Metal ions and water
choices.why: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds between neighboring backbones, N–H to O.

explanation: The secondary structure of a protein involves hydrogen bonds between neighboring polypeptide backbones: hydrogens bonded to nitrogen in one backbone bond to oxygen atoms in another. Individually weak, they stabilize the structure because they repeat many times.
